subtopics.name: Upper GI disorders and GI bleeding

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) has nighttime heartburn and a cough. The nurse reviews lifestyle changes. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll put blocks under the head of my bed to raise it."
"I'll have my evening snack right before I go to bed."
"I'll cut back on coffee, chocolate and peppermint tea."
"I'll eat smaller meals and try to lose some weight."

rationale.correct: GERD: avoid lying down after meals, raise the head of the bed, avoid triggers and lose weight if needed.

perOption.a: Elevation reduces nighttime reflux.
perOption.b: Eating within 2 to 3 hours of lying down increases reflux.
perOption.c: These relax the lower esophageal sphincter.
perOption.d: Smaller meals and weight loss reduce stomach pressure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a duodenal ulcer caused by Helicobacter pylori is prescribed amoxicillin, clarithromycin and omeprazole for 14 days. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll take every pill for 14 days, even once I feel better."
"I'll stop the antibiotics once my stomach pain goes away."
"The omeprazole is the main medicine; the others are extra."
"I'll take ibuprofen for any pain while I'm on these pills."

rationale.correct: H. pylori therapy combines antibiotics with acid suppression; the client completes the full course.

perOption.a: Completing therapy eradicates H. pylori and prevents the ulcer from returning.
perOption.b: Stopping early allows recurrence and resistance.
perOption.c: The antibiotics are needed to eliminate the infection.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach adherence to H. pylori therapy.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old client with a history of peptic ulcer disease who takes naproxen daily suddenly has severe epigastric pain that spreads across the abdomen. The abdomen is rigid, the client lies very still, and the heart rate is 118/min. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Perforation of the ulcer
A flare of reflux esophagitis
Pyloric obstruction from scarring
Expected ulcer pain after a meal

rationale.correct: Perforation: sudden severe pain, a rigid abdomen and signs of shock; keep the client NPO and notify the provider at once.

perOption.a: Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen suggests perforation with peritonitis, a surgical emergency.
perOption.b: GERD causes burning, not a rigid abdomen.
perOption.c: Obstruction causes vomiting and fullness, not a board-like abdomen.
perOption.d: Ulcer pain does not cause a rigid abdomen and tachycardia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder is vomiting coffee-ground material. The heart rate is 120/min, the blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg, and the client is anxious. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Insert two large-bore IVs and start fluids as prescribed
Give a dose of liquid antacid to coat the stomach
Call the endoscopy unit to schedule a scope tomorrow
Offer sips of cold water to settle the nausea

rationale.correct: Upper GI bleed: ABCs, large-bore IV access, fluids and blood, a proton pump inhibitor and urgent endoscopy.

perOption.a: Restoring volume treats the hypovolemic shock from bleeding.
perOption.b: This does not address shock.
perOption.c: Endoscopy is urgent and follows stabilization.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Stabilize a client with an upper GI bleed.

questions.stem: A client with erosive esophagitis is prescribed omeprazole 20 mg daily. The client usually eats breakfast at 0700 and takes all medicines with dinner. When should the nurse teach the client to take the omeprazole?

options.text: Around 0630, before breakfast
With dinner, along with the other medicines
At bedtime with a small snack
On the days when heartburn occurs

rationale.correct: PPIs: take before breakfast; long-term use is linked with C. difficile, fractures and low magnesium.

perOption.a: PPIs work best when taken 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal of the day.
perOption.b: Taking it with food reduces its effect.
perOption.c: This is not the best timing.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach timing for proton pump inhibitors.

questions.stem: A client with a gastric ulcer is prescribed sucralfate 1 g four times a day and also takes levothyroxine and an antacid. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Take it on an empty stomach, 2 hours apart from other drugs."
"Take it at the same time as the antacid so they work together."
"Take the four doses together at bedtime for convenience."
"Chew the tablet with a glass of milk to protect the ulcer."

rationale.correct: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier; take it 1 hour before meals and separate it from other drugs.

perOption.a: Sucralfate coats ulcers and can bind other drugs, reducing their absorption.
perOption.b: Antacids interfere with sucralfate.
perOption.c: It is usually taken before meals and at bedtime.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who had a partial gastrectomy 3 weeks ago reports cramping, sweating and a racing heart 20 minutes after meals. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of how to manage this?

options.text: "I'll eat small, high-protein meals and drink between meals."
"I'll drink a large glass of juice with each meal."
"I'll take a brisk walk right after I finish eating each meal."
"I'll eat three large meals so I'm not eating all day."

rationale.correct: Dumping syndrome: small, frequent, low-carbohydrate meals, fluids between meals and lying down after eating.

perOption.a: This slows gastric emptying and prevents fluid shifts.
perOption.b: Fluids and sugar with meals worsen dumping.
perOption.c: Lying down after meals slows emptying.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach dietary management of dumping syndrome.

questions.stem: A small-bore nasogastric feeding tube has just been inserted for a client who had a stroke. The first feeding is prescribed. Which method should the nurse use to confirm placement before the first feeding?

options.text: A chest or abdominal x-ray
Listening over the stomach while injecting air
Placing the end of the tube in a cup of water
Asking the client to speak or hum

rationale.correct: Confirm initial placement by x-ray; at the bedside afterward, check gastric aspirate pH (5 or less) and the external tube length.

perOption.a: An x-ray is the most reliable way to confirm initial placement.
perOption.b: This method is unreliable.
perOption.c: This is unsafe and unreliable.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is receiving a continuous tube feeding at 60 mL/hr. Which action by assistive personnel requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Lays the bed flat to change linens with the feeding running
Keeps the head of the bed at 35 degrees through the whole shift
Tells the nurse that the client has started coughing
Records the volume infused at the end of the shift

rationale.correct: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or higher during feedings, and pause the feeding if the client must lie flat.

perOption.a: Lying flat with the feeding running increases aspiration risk; the feeding is paused first.
perOption.b: This is correct.
perOption.c: This is appropriate to report.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client who had abdominal surgery 2 years ago has had crampy abdominal pain and vomiting since last night. Which findings suggest a small bowel obstruction?

options.text: Distention with high-pitched bowel sounds
Bloody diarrhea with lower abdominal pain
Weight gain with constipation over months
Burning chest pain after spicy meals

rationale.correct: Bowel obstruction: distention, crampy pain, vomiting and changing bowel sounds; managed with NG decompression and NPO status.

perOption.a: Early obstruction causes high-pitched bowel sounds above the blockage, distention and vomiting.
perOption.b: This suggests colitis.
perOption.c: This is not an acute obstruction.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for two clients with inflammatory bowel disease, one with ulcerative colitis and one with Crohn disease, and is preparing to teach both clients about their condition. For each feature, choose the condition it is more typical of.

rows.text: Continuous inflammation that starts in the rectum
Skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus
Can be cured by removing the colon

rationale.correct: UC: continuous, colon only, mucosal and bloody. Crohn disease: skip lesions, full thickness, anywhere in the GI tract, with fistulas.

perOption.r1:c1: UC spreads continuously from the rectum.
perOption.r1:c2: Crohn disease has patchy skip lesions.
perOption.r2:c1: UC is limited to the colon and rectum.
perOption.r2:c2: Crohn disease can affect any part of the GI tract.
perOption.r3:c1: Bloody diarrhea is typical of UC.
perOption.r3:c2: Crohn diarrhea is usually less bloody.
perOption.r4:c2: Inflammation through the full bowel wall causes fistulas.
perOption.r5:c1: Colectomy removes the disease in UC.
perOption.r5:c2: Crohn disease can recur elsewhere after surgery.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell ulcerative colitis apart from Crohn disease.

questions.stem: A client with a severe flare of Crohn disease has 10 liquid stools a day, a new enterocutaneous fistula, an albumin of 2.4 g/dL and a 7 kg weight loss. Which nutrition plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Bowel rest with parenteral nutrition
A high-fiber diet to bulk up the stools
A high-fat diet to increase calories
A regular diet with extra dairy for protein

rationale.correct: Severe IBD flare with fistula or malnutrition: bowel rest with parenteral nutrition; milder flares use a low-residue, high-protein diet.

perOption.a: Bowel rest lets the fistula and bowel heal while PN meets high protein and calorie needs.
perOption.b: Fiber worsens diarrhea and cramping during a flare.
perOption.c: Fat may worsen diarrhea.
perOption.d: Lactose intolerance is common, and the bowel needs rest.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan nutrition during an IBD flare.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old client is going home after recovering from an episode of acute diverticulitis treated with bowel rest and antibiotics. Which diet should the nurse teach to help prevent further episodes?

options.text: A high-fiber diet with plenty of fluids
A low-fiber diet for the rest of the client's life
Clear liquids whenever the client feels bloated
A high-fat diet to keep the stool soft

rationale.correct: Acute diverticulitis: bowel rest and antibiotics. Prevention: a high-fiber diet with fluids.

perOption.a: Fiber softens stool and lowers pressure in the colon.
perOption.b: Low fiber is used only during the acute phase.
perOption.c: Clear liquids are for acute episodes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old client admitted with suspected appendicitis rates right lower abdominal pain as 7 out of 10 and asks for a heating pad. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that heat is avoided; offer a cold pack if prescribed
Place a heating pad on the lower abdomen on the low setting for comfort
Give the PRN laxative to relieve any constipation
Give a small enema to relieve abdominal pressure

rationale.correct: Suspected appendicitis: avoid heat, laxatives and enemas; keep the client NPO and prepare for surgery.

perOption.a: Heat may increase inflammation and the risk of rupture.
perOption.b: Heat is not recommended.
perOption.c: Laxatives can cause perforation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client at average risk for colorectal cancer has never been screened and says, "I'll wait until I'm 50, like my father did." What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "Screening for average-risk adults now starts at age 45."
"You're right; screening for most people starts at 50."
"Screening isn't needed unless you notice blood in the stool."
"You should wait until 60 if you have no family history."

rationale.correct: Colorectal screening starts at 45 for average-risk adults, by colonoscopy every 10 years or another approved test.

perOption.a: Current recommendations start screening for average-risk adults at 45.
perOption.b: The starting age was lowered to 45.
perOption.c: Screening is for people without symptoms.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the starting age for colorectal cancer screening.

questions.stem: A client is preparing at home for a colonoscopy tomorrow morning. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll stick to clear liquids for the whole day today."
"I'll have red gelatin and grape juice tonight."
"I'll drink all of the bowel prep, even if it's hard."
"My sister will drive me home after the test."

rationale.correct: Colonoscopy prep: clear liquids, no red or purple dyes, the complete bowel prep and a ride home.

perOption.a: This is correct.
perOption.b: Red and purple liquids can look like blood in the colon.
perOption.c: A complete prep allows a clear view.
perOption.d: Sedation is used, so a ride home is needed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing four clients with new ostomies on the first day after surgery. Which stoma finding should the nurse report to the surgeon right away?

options.text: A moist, beefy red stoma with mucus
A pink stoma that bleeds slightly when cleaned
A stoma that has turned dark purple to black
A stoma that is slightly swollen and shiny

rationale.correct: A healthy stoma is moist and red-pink; a dusky or black stoma needs immediate attention.

perOption.a: This is a healthy stoma.
perOption.b: Slight bleeding when cleaned is normal.
perOption.c: This indicates poor blood supply and necrosis.
perOption.d: Edema is expected in the first days.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with a new ileostomy for ulcerative colitis is going home. The output has been 1,200 mL a day of liquid stool. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: Drink plenty of fluids and watch for signs of dehydration
Irrigate the ileostomy each morning to make the output regular
Expect the stool to become formed within a few weeks
Limit fluids so that the output is lower

rationale.correct: Ileostomy: a high risk of fluid and electrolyte loss; chew food well and watch for blockage.

perOption.a: Ileostomy output is liquid and contains electrolytes, so dehydration is a major risk.
perOption.b: Ileostomies are not irrigated.
perOption.c: Ileostomy output stays liquid to pasty.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to cut the skin barrier for a new colostomy pouch. How large should the opening be compared with the stoma?

options.text: About 2 to 3 mm (1/8 inch) larger than the stoma
Exactly the same size, so no skin shows
About 2.5 cm (1 inch) larger, for comfort
Slightly smaller, so the seal is tight

rationale.correct: Cut the barrier about 1/8 inch larger than the stoma to protect the skin.

perOption.a: This protects the skin without squeezing the stoma.
perOption.b: This can injure the stoma.
perOption.c: Too much skin is exposed to stool.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client in assisted living has had hard stools every 4 to 5 days for months and takes a stimulant laxative most days. The client drinks about 800 mL a day. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Increase fiber and fluids and stay as active as possible
Keep taking the stimulant laxative each day
Wait to use the toilet until the urge is strong
Drink less so that the bladder is not overworked

rationale.correct: Prevent constipation with fiber, fluids, activity and responding promptly to the urge.

perOption.a: These promote regular bowel movements.
perOption.b: Daily stimulant use can cause dependence.
perOption.c: Ignoring or delaying the urge worsens constipation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with cancer pain is starting long-acting oxycodone twice a day. Which bowel regimen should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A stool softener plus a stimulant laxative, started now
A bulk-forming laxative alone, with fluids limited to 1 L a day
No regimen unless constipation develops later in treatment
A daily soapsuds enema to keep the bowel empty

rationale.correct: Opioid-induced constipation does not resolve with time; start a preventive regimen with the opioid.

perOption.a: Opioids slow the bowel, so preventive treatment is started at once.
perOption.b: Bulk without enough fluid can cause impaction.
perOption.c: Prevention is recommended.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with chemotherapy-induced nausea is receiving IV ondansetron and also takes citalopram for depression and methadone for chronic pain. Which finding is most important for the nurse to monitor?

options.text: The QT interval on the ECG
The capillary blood glucose
Hearing and balance
The color of the urine

rationale.correct: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, especially with other QT-prolonging drugs; it also causes headache and constipation.

perOption.a: Ondansetron, citalopram and methadone can each prolong the QT interval and cause dysrhythmias.
perOption.b: This is not the key concern.
perOption.c: This is not the key concern.
perOption.d: This is not the key concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the third day after an open colectomy, a client has a distended, tympanic abdomen, no bowel sounds in any quadrant, no flatus and nausea. The client is taking IV morphine and has a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Paralytic ileus
Expected recovery after abdominal surgery
Leak at the bowel anastomosis
Clostridioides difficile colitis

rationale.correct: Paralytic ileus: NPO, NG decompression if needed, early walking, fewer opioids and correction of electrolytes.

perOption.a: Reduced peristalsis after surgery, worsened by opioids and low potassium, causes absent bowel sounds and distention.
perOption.b: Absent bowel sounds with distention are not expected by day 3.
perOption.c: A leak usually causes fever, increasing pain and signs of peritonitis.
perOption.d: This causes diarrhea, not absent bowel sounds.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with dysphagia after a stroke is to receive 1,440 mL of enteral formula continuously over 24 hours through a gastrostomy tube, with 30 mL water flushes every 4 hours. The client weighs 70 kg and the head of the bed is at 35 degrees. At what rate should the nurse set the feeding pump?

rationale.correct: Rate = 1,440 mL ÷ 24 hr = 60 mL/hr. The water flushes are given separately and are not part of the formula rate.
references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a continuous tube feeding rate.

questions.stem: The nurse is inserting a nasogastric tube for decompression in a client with a bowel obstruction. Place the steps in order, from first to last.

items.text: Measure the tube from the tip of the nose to the earlobe to the xiphoid process
Confirm placement before using the tube
Insert the tube through the nostril with the head tilted slightly back
Have the client tilt the head forward and swallow as the tube is advanced
Lubricate the tip of the tube

rationale.correct: Measure, lubricate, insert, flex and swallow, then confirm placement.

perOption.a: Measuring sets how far to insert the tube.
perOption.b: Lubrication makes insertion easier and reduces trauma.
perOption.c: This follows the natural curve of the nasopharynx.
perOption.d: Flexing the neck and swallowing guide the tube into the esophagus.
perOption.e: Placement is verified before use to prevent aspiration.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Insert a nasogastric tube in the correct sequence.
